meta.name: ReUnite Dog Knowledge Base
meta.purpose: General educational dog-care guidance. Not a veterinary diagnosis or substitute for professional care.

emergencies.answer: 🚨 EMERGENCY: Trouble breathing, choking, blue/gray gums, collapse, or unconsciousness can be life-threatening. Keep your dog as calm and still as possible and contact an emergency veterinarian immediately. Do not delay care while trying home remedies.

🚨 EMERGENCY: Heavy bleeding that does not stop with firm, gentle pressure needs urgent veterinary care. Use clean gauze or cloth to apply steady pressure while arranging transport. Do not remove deeply embedded objects.

🚨 Seizure: Move nearby objects away so your dog cannot injure itself, keep hands away from the mouth, and time the episode. Seek emergency veterinary help for a first seizure, repeated seizures, a seizure lasting several minutes, or poor recovery afterward.

🚨 POSSIBLE POISONING: Contact a veterinarian or animal poison service immediately. Keep the product/package and note what was eaten, roughly how much, and when. Do not induce vomiting or give a home antidote unless a veterinary professional specifically tells you to.

🚨 POSSIBLE HEATSTROKE: Move the dog to a cool area and contact a veterinarian urgently. Use cool—not ice-cold—water to help lower body temperature while arranging care. Weakness, confusion, collapse, vomiting, or abnormal breathing are emergency signs.

🚨 POSSIBLE BLOAT/GDV: A suddenly swollen or painful abdomen, repeated unproductive retching, restlessness, weakness, or collapse is an emergency. Go to an emergency veterinarian immediately. Do not wait to see if it passes.

topics.name: vomiting
topics.answer: Vomiting can have many causes, from dietary upset to illness or poisoning. Keep track of how often it happens and whether there is blood, severe pain, weakness, diarrhea, or inability to keep water down. Repeated vomiting, blood, marked weakness, or suspected poisoning warrants prompt veterinary advice. Do not give human medicines unless a veterinarian tells you to.

topics.name: diarrhea
topics.answer: Mild diarrhea can occur after diet changes or minor stomach upset, but persistent or severe diarrhea can cause dehydration. Watch hydration, energy, appetite, and stool appearance. Blood/black stool, repeated vomiting, severe weakness, significant pain, or diarrhea in a very young/old or medically fragile dog should prompt veterinary care.

topics.name: not eating
topics.answer: A reduced appetite can have many causes, including stress, dental pain, stomach upset, infection, or other illness. Note how long your dog has refused food and whether it is drinking and acting normally. If appetite loss is sudden, persistent, or accompanied by vomiting, pain, weakness, breathing changes, or other concerning signs, contact a veterinarian.

topics.name: dehydration
topics.answer: Watch for unusual lethargy, dry or tacky gums, reduced urination, or worsening weakness. Encourage normal access to fresh water, but do not force large amounts at once if the dog is vomiting. Suspected significant dehydration needs veterinary assessment.

topics.name: cough
topics.answer: Coughing can be caused by irritation, infection, airway disease, heart problems, or other conditions. Note when it happens and whether there is fever, nasal discharge, breathing difficulty, weakness, or exercise intolerance. Breathing difficulty or blue/gray gums is an emergency.

topics.name: itching
topics.answer: Itching can come from fleas/ticks, allergies, skin infection, parasites, or irritation. Check the skin and coat for fleas, redness, sores, odor, or hair loss. Persistent or severe itching, open wounds, facial swelling, or breathing changes should be evaluated by a veterinarian.

topics.name: fleas ticks
topics.answer: Use only flea/tick products that are specifically labeled for your dog's species, age, weight, and situation. Never substitute a product for another species without veterinary advice. Check the whole coat regularly and ask a veterinarian about a safe prevention plan.

topics.name: ear problems
topics.answer: Ear redness, odor, discharge, frequent scratching, or head shaking can indicate an ear problem. Avoid putting household liquids or cotton swabs deep into the ear. A veterinarian can examine the ear and determine the cause and appropriate treatment.

topics.name: eye problems
topics.answer: Eye problems can worsen quickly. Redness, squinting, pain, swelling, injury, cloudiness, or significant discharge should be assessed by a veterinarian, especially if sudden. Avoid using leftover human or pet eye medicines unless prescribed for this episode.

topics.name: wound
topics.answer: For a small superficial wound, gently rinse with clean water and prevent licking. Do not use harsh chemicals or human creams unless a veterinarian recommends them. Deep wounds, bites, heavy contamination, uncontrolled bleeding, severe pain, or swelling need veterinary care.

topics.name: paw
topics.answer: Check the paw for cuts, foreign material, swelling, or a broken nail. Keep activity gentle and prevent licking. Persistent limping, severe pain, a suspected fracture, deep wound, or uncontrolled bleeding should be assessed by a veterinarian.

topics.name: dental
topics.answer: Dental disease is common in dogs. Regular brushing with dog-safe toothpaste and veterinary dental checks can help. Never use human toothpaste. Bleeding gums, facial swelling, severe mouth pain, or difficulty eating should be checked by a veterinarian.

topics.name: vaccination
topics.answer: Vaccination schedules depend on age, local disease risk, lifestyle, and previous vaccine history. Puppies usually need a series of core vaccinations, followed by boosters according to veterinary guidance. Your veterinarian can create the right schedule for your dog.

topics.name: deworming
topics.answer: Parasite prevention should be based on your dog's age, lifestyle, local risks, and veterinary advice. Different parasites need different treatments, so avoid choosing a dewormer only from symptoms. Ask a veterinarian about an appropriate prevention and testing plan.

topics.name: nutrition
topics.answer: A balanced, complete dog food appropriate for your dog's life stage is a good foundation. Fresh water should always be available. Treats should be limited and table scraps can be risky. For allergies, medical conditions, homemade diets, or major weight changes, consult a veterinarian or veterinary nutrition professional.

topics.name: toxic foods
topics.answer: Important foods to keep away from dogs include chocolate/cocoa, xylitol (an artificial sweetener), grapes and raisins, onions/garlic in concentrated amounts, alcohol, and some other foods or products. If your dog may have eaten a toxic substance, contact a veterinarian promptly rather than waiting for symptoms.

topics.name: puppy care
topics.answer: Puppies need age-appropriate nutrition, vaccinations, parasite prevention, safe socialization, sleep, and gentle positive-reinforcement training. Keep hazardous objects and toxic foods out of reach. Your veterinarian can guide vaccination, deworming, diet, and growth monitoring.

topics.name: senior dog
topics.answer: Senior dogs benefit from regular veterinary checkups, weight monitoring, dental care, appropriate exercise, and attention to changes in appetite, thirst, mobility, sleep, or behavior. New changes should not simply be assumed to be 'old age'; discuss them with a veterinarian.

topics.name: grooming
topics.answer: Regular brushing, safe nail trimming, coat care, and appropriate bathing help maintain skin and coat health. Use dog-specific products and avoid getting shampoo or other products in the eyes and ears. Skin odor, sores, persistent dandruff, or severe matting may need veterinary advice.

topics.name: exercise
topics.answer: Exercise needs vary by age, breed, health, and temperament. Use gradual, appropriate activity and provide rest, water, and heat protection. Puppies and dogs with health problems may need special limits. Stop activity and seek veterinary advice if your dog shows breathing trouble, collapse, severe weakness, or unusual pain.

topics.name: behavior
topics.answer: Use reward-based training, predictable routines, safe management, and gradual exposure rather than punishment. Sudden behavior changes can sometimes have a medical cause. For aggression, serious bite risk, or severe anxiety, work with a qualified veterinarian and/or certified behavior professional.

topics.name: heat safety
topics.answer: Provide shade, fresh water, ventilation, and cooler activity times. Avoid strenuous exercise during hot periods and never leave a dog in a parked car. Heavy panting with weakness, confusion, vomiting, collapse, or abnormal breathing is an emergency.

topics.name: travel
topics.answer: For travel, use a secure harness or crate, carry identification and medical/vaccine records, bring water and familiar items, and plan breaks. Never leave a dog unattended in a vehicle. Check destination rules and veterinary needs before a longer trip.
